1044.title: Women's ordination
1044.hook: the debate over full ordination for women, told from both sides with respect
1044.howItsDone: Fully ordained nuns live and teach in East Asian Buddhist communities; in Theravada and Tibetan communities, women practice as novices, as precept-holding nuns, or in newer bhikkhuni communities, and the question is discussed by monks, nuns and lay people.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ambedkar and a movement that measured worth by deeds, not birth. Your line: a path of dignity. Whose name did you learn or use? Day one thousand forty-four.

Here's an odd thing about today's argument. Two people who disagree sharply can open the same text, the long account of the Buddha's final months, and each find a line for their side. One reads a warning about changing rules that were laid down. The other reads the Buddha naming who belongs in his community. The question is whether women can be fully ordained as nuns, bhikkhunis, in traditions where that line was lost. Today both sides get to speak, each at its best.
screen: `ONE TEXT, TWO SIDES.` → `A RULE KEPT AS LAID DOWN.` → `WHO BELONGS IN THE COMMUNITY.`

segments.voice: As this path told some weeks ago, the Vinaya says the order of nuns began with Mahapajapati. Lines of fully ordained nuns continue in Chinese, Korean and Vietnamese communities, and those nuns are part of daily temple life. In Theravada lands the line broke, and Tibetan communities have had no unbroken line of their own. So here is the first side, at its best. Early in that long discourse, the Buddha tells his monks they can expect to prosper as long as they don't lay down rules that were never laid down, and don't throw out rules that were. The Vinaya says a nun is ordained by a sangha of nuns and then by a sangha of monks. For monks who hold this view, if the nuns' sangha is gone, no one now has the standing to make a new one, and inventing a way around the rule would be just what that discourse warns against. Keeping the form whole is how they keep faith with the Buddha. Now the second side, at its best. Later in the same discourse, Mara urges the Buddha to pass away, and the Buddha says he won't go until his monks, his nuns, and his lay men and lay women have learned the teaching. To supporters of restoring the order, that is the Buddha naming four assemblies, nuns among them, as the shape of his community. Some Theravada women have received full ordination with nuns from East Asian lines taking part, and some monks have stood with them. Notice what the two sides share: each is trying to be faithful, and each points to the Buddha's own words. The canon even has a talk for moments like this, the Kinti Sutta. When monks disagree about meaning, it advises going to them gently, showing exactly where the difference lies, and not letting it become a quarrel.
screen: `ONE SIDE: KEEP RULES AS LAID DOWN.` · `THE OTHER: NUNS AMONG FOUR ASSEMBLIES.` · `BOTH POINT TO THE BUDDHA'S WORDS.` · then, large: `NAME THE DIFFERENCE, NOT A QUARREL.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, if you'd like: listen to both sides. Sit and settle. Pick a question you have strong feelings about, any question. First, for a few breaths, let the side you agree with speak in your mind, at its best. Then let the other side speak, also at its best, as its wisest supporter would put it, not as a cartoon. Notice what happens in your body as you listen. Tightening? Softening? You don't have to change your mind. Just let both sides finish their sentences. The bell holds the time.
Women's ordination. The question of whether women may again be fully ordained as bhikkhunis where the line was lost, argued by people on both sides who quote the same teacher. Today's word.
Your line: told with respect. Today, when you disagree with someone, try saying their view back to them in a way they'd agree with, before you give yours. Day one thousand forty-four.

1045.title: Trust broken
1045.hook: abuses of power in some Western and Asian centers, and the communities that faced them
1045.howItsDone: Some Buddhist centers now publish ethics codes, name contacts outside the teacher for raising concerns, and ask outside investigators to look into complaints; Theravada monastic communities hold the pavarana at the end of the rains retreat, inviting one another to point out faults.

segments.voice: Yesterday, women's ordination, and two sides who love the same teacher. Your line: told with respect. Did you say someone's view back to them before giving yours? Day one thousand forty-five.

The teacher sits on a raised cushion at the front of the hall. Students bow when the teacher enters. The teacher's word on practice is final, and people have rearranged their lives to be near the teacher. Often, that trust is a gift. It lets a student go deep. But trust is also power, and power can be misused. Today's history is uncomfortable, and it belongs in an honest course: what happened when trust was broken in some Buddhist communities, and what those communities did next.
screen: `A TEACHER ON A RAISED CUSHION.` → `TRUST IS ALSO POWER.` → `WHEN IT WAS BROKEN.`

segments.voice: In some Buddhist centers, in Asia and in the West, teachers have misused the trust placed in them: sexual misconduct with students, bullying, money taken or hidden. People who were harmed have described how hard it was to be heard, because the teacher was respected and the community wanted to protect its practice. This path looked at the warning signs some weeks ago. Today is about what comes after, when someone speaks. The Vinaya has a ceremony built for exactly that. At the end of the rains retreat, each monk, the most senior first, faces the others and invites them: about anything they have seen, or heard, or suspected, he asks them to speak to him, out of compassion, so that he can make amends. It's called the pavarana, the invitation. It takes for granted that anyone, however senior, may need correcting, and it puts that on the calendar. There's a second teaching, about how to speak. In a discourse to a prince named Abhaya, the Buddha says he won't say what is false or useless, however welcome it would be. What is true and beneficial, he says, he will say even when it's unwelcome, and he knows the right time to say it. True, useful, and timed with care. Communities that faced abuse have tried to build both into their life. They listened to the people who were harmed, and took them seriously enough to look. They brought in outside investigators. Some teachers stepped down. Groups wrote ethics codes, named people other than the teacher to receive concerns, and went to the police when a crime was involved. None of it undoes the harm. But it can make the room safer for the next student.
screen: `WHEN TRUST WAS MISUSED.` · `PAVARANA: PLEASE TELL ME.` · `TRUE, USEFUL, AT THE RIGHT TIME.` · then, large: `MAKE THE ROOM SAFER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, if you'd like: know how to raise a concern. Sit and take a few steady breaths. Think of a group you belong to: a center, a congregation, a team, a club. Ask quietly: if something were wrong here, who would I tell? Is there someone besides the person in charge? Is there a written way to report it? If you don't know, notice that, without alarm, and make a note to find out. If someone comes to mind who might need help right now, breathe with that, and know that a trusted person or the local authorities can be called. The bell holds the time.
Trust broken. When teachers in some Buddhist communities misused their power, and the communities learned to listen, investigate and make things safer. Today's word.
Your line: speak up safely. Today, find out one thing: where, in a group you belong to, a concern could be raised with someone other than the person in charge. Day one thousand forty-five.

1046.title: Mindfulness everywhere
1046.hook: meditation in hospitals, schools and offices: what it gives, and what can be lost when ethics are left out
1046.howItsDone: In Buddhist settings, mindfulness is taught alongside the precepts, loving-kindness and the rest of the path; in secular programs, it's taught as attention training, and some programs add kindness practices.

segments.voice: Yesterday, trust broken, and the communities that learned to listen and make things safer. Your line: speak up safely. Did you find out who you could tell? Day one thousand forty-six.

A phone buzzes in the middle of the afternoon: time for a mindful minute. A nurse on a break sits in a quiet room with an audio track. A class of children puts their hands on their bellies and counts breaths before a test. An office books a meditation session between budget meetings. A practice that grew up in monasteries now turns up in hospitals, schools and offices, without robes, bells or Buddhist words. Today asks a fair question: what does it bring with it, and what might it leave behind?
screen: `A MINDFUL MINUTE ON YOUR PHONE.` → `HOSPITALS, SCHOOLS, OFFICES.` → `WHAT CAME ALONG, WHAT WAS LEFT?`

segments.voice: The Pali word usually translated as mindfulness is sati. In the Buddha's teaching on the foundations of mindfulness, it means steady, clear awareness of the body, of feelings, of the mind and of how things arise and pass. Teachers in hospitals and clinics took practices like these and offered them without religious language, to help people living with pain, stress and illness. Some people say it has helped them, and researchers have studied it, which is tomorrow's story. Supporters, including some Buddhist teachers, see this as a door opened wide: people who would never walk into a temple can still learn to sit with their breath. And some of these programs do teach kindness alongside attention. But some Buddhist teachers and scholars have raised a worry. In the path as the old texts lay it out, mindfulness doesn't stand alone. Right mindfulness is one part of the path, alongside right speech, right action and right livelihood, right intention and right effort. Attention by itself is a tool, and a tool can serve anything. You can be very focused while doing something harmful. In the path, sati is held inside sila, ethical conduct, and inside compassion, so that what you notice turns into how you treat people. Both sides want the same good thing: less suffering. One says start where people are, and the rest may follow. The other says keep the whole path in view, or the practice can be bent to other ends. Today's line holds both: the breath at your desk, and the ethics around it.
screen: `SATI: STEADY, CLEAR AWARENESS.` · `A DOOR OPENED WIDE.` · `ATTENTION ALONE IS A TOOL.` · then, large: `MINDFULNESS INSIDE THE WHOLE PATH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, if you'd like: keep kindness with your mindfulness. Sit and settle. For the first part, simply feel the breath: in at the nose, the belly rising and falling. When the mind wanders, notice and come back. Then, without dropping the breath, add one thing. Bring to mind someone you'll see later today, and with each out-breath, let a wish go to them: may your day go well. Attention, with kindness riding on it. If you lose the breath, start again from the breath. The bell holds the time.
Mindfulness everywhere. Sati carried into hospitals, schools and offices, with the question of whether the ethics travel with it. Today's word.
Your line: keep the ethics. Today, after any moment of focus, at work, on a screen, at the stove, ask one quick question: who does this help? Day one thousand forty-six.

1047.title: Science and meditation
1047.hook: researchers and practitioners in conversation; claims checked carefully
1047.howItsDone: Some Buddhist teachers and monastics take part in research and dialogue with scientists, and some practitioners read studies on meditation with interest while saying the path's aim goes beyond what a lab can measure.

segments.voice: Yesterday, mindfulness everywhere: in hospitals, schools and offices, and what slips away when the ethics are left behind. Your line: keep the ethics. Did kindness travel with your attention? Day one thousand forty-seven.

A monk in maroon robes sits very still in a research lab, a cap of small sensors on his head, while a scientist watches a screen in the next room. Afterward they sit down together, and the conversation runs both ways. The scientist asks what the monk was doing inside. The monk asks what the screen can and can't show. Meetings like that have happened, and they raise a question for anyone on this path: when someone makes a claim about meditation, how do you know if it's true? Today's answer has two parts, and one of them is very old.
screen: `A MONK IN A LAB.` → `THE QUESTIONS RUN BOTH WAYS.` → `HOW DO YOU KNOW?`

segments.voice: Start with the old part. This block has heard the Buddha's advice to the Kalamas more than once. Here's a bolder one, from the Majjhima Nikaya, a discourse called the Inquirer. The Buddha tells his monks that someone who can't see into another's mind should investigate even him, the Buddha, to find out whether he really is awake. Watch what can be seen and heard of him, the sutta says, and look again over time: does anything harmful turn up? Does he change once he's famous? Trust built that way, it says, has reasons under it and is firm. The old recollection of the teaching puts that spirit into one word: ehipassiko, come and see. Now the new part. Researchers have studied meditation, and some Buddhist teachers, the Dalai Lama among them, have spent long hours in conversation with scientists. Some careful researchers say plainly that the results are mixed and that headlines often run ahead of the findings. A careful study summary tells you a few things. Who was studied. What they were compared with. How large the change was. And what wasn't found. Some practitioners welcome all this. Others add a gentle warning: the Buddha's aim was freedom from suffering, and a lab can measure a calmer pulse but not everything the path is for. The two points can sit side by side. The Inquirer isn't a lab manual, and old texts can be stretched too far. But if a sutta asks people to check even the Buddha, checking a headline about meditation is in the same spirit: hear the claim, look closely, and test it against what actually happens.
screen: `INVESTIGATE EVEN THE TEACHER.` · `EHIPASSIKO: COME AND SEE.` · `RESULTS ARE OFTEN MIXED.` · then, large: `WHO, COMPARED WITH WHAT, HOW MUCH?`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, if you'd like: become a careful reader for two minutes. Sit, and let the breath settle. Bring to mind one thing you've heard about meditation. It lowers stress. It changes the brain. It makes you happier. Hold that claim lightly, the way you'd hold a stone you found on a path. Ask it quietly: who said so? Compared with what? Then let it go and simply watch the breath, which you can check for yourself, right now. After the bell, find one careful summary of a meditation study and read it slowly. The bell holds the time.
Ehipassiko. Come and see — the old word whose spirit guides researchers and practitioners in conversation now, with every claim held up to the light. Today's word.

Your line: checked carefully. Today, when a headline makes a big promise about anything, health or happiness or the mind, pause and ask one question before you share it: compared with what? Day one thousand forty-seven.

1048.title: Ordaining trees
1048.hook: in Thailand, monks wrap trees in robes to protect forests from logging
1048.howItsDone: In parts of Thailand, monks and villagers hold tree ordination ceremonies, wrapping trees in saffron cloth with chanting and offerings to mark a forest as protected; some monasteries also plant trees and care for forest land.

segments.voice: Yesterday, science and meditation, and ehipassiko, the sutta's call to check even the Buddha. Your line: checked carefully. Did a headline get a second look? Day one thousand forty-eight.

A strip of saffron cloth, the color of a monk's robe, is wrapped around the trunk of a big old tree at the edge of a forest in Thailand. Monks chant. Villagers stand around with offerings. Someone ties the knot. From then on, people in the village speak of that tree differently, and a logger with a chainsaw may stop and think twice. The tree, they say, has been ordained. It's a strange-sounding idea at first, a tree becoming a monk, and today we find out what it's really doing.
screen: `SAFFRON CLOTH ON A TRUNK.` → `MONKS CHANT, VILLAGERS WATCH.` → `THE TREE HAS BEEN ORDAINED.`

segments.voice: First, what the ceremony is for. In parts of Thailand, forests that villages relied on for water, food and shade were being cut down. Some monks, especially in the countryside, began holding ceremonies that wrap a robe around a tree, and sometimes around many trees in a forest. The monks who do it don't claim a tree can really take the precepts. It's a sign. The robe says this forest is held in the same care as the sangha, and harming it is a serious thing. Second, why it fits the tradition. The monastic rules, the Vinaya, already ask monks not to destroy plant life. And trees run through the Buddha's own story. Tradition places his birth in a garden, under a tree. He woke up under a tree, the one later called the bodhi tree. And the Mahaparinibbana Sutta tells of his passing between twin sala trees. Some suttas close with a plain instruction to the monks, in paraphrase: here are the roots of trees, here are empty huts. Meditate. Third, the cost. Monks who led these ceremonies were sometimes told they were meddling in politics, and some faced pressure for it. Communities have argued over whether this is the sangha's work at all. Last, an old line from the Dhammapada, in Max Müller's translation: "As the bee collects nectar and departs without injuring the flower, or its colour or scent, so let a sage dwell in his village." The ordained tree is that line in cloth. Take what you need, and leave the flower whole.
screen: `A ROBE AROUND A TREE IS A SIGN.` · `THE VINAYA PROTECTS PLANT LIFE.` · `BORN, AWAKE, GONE, UNDER TREES.` · then, large: `AS THE BEE COLLECTS NECTAR.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, if you'd like: care for one tree. Sit comfortably and let the breath settle. Bring to mind a tree you know. The one outside your window, on your street, in a park, from your childhood. See its bark, its shape, how it moves in wind. Breathe in, and remember that its leaves breathe this same air. Breathe out, and let a little thanks go toward it. Then choose one small act for that tree today: water it, clear the trash from around its roots, or just stand under it for a minute. The bell holds the time.

Ordaining trees. In Thailand, monks wrap saffron robes around trees to mark a forest as protected, a sign drawn from the Vinaya's care for plant life and the trees of the Buddha's own story. Today's word.
Your line: the ordained tree. Today, before you throw away paper or buy something wrapped in it, picture a strip of saffron cloth around a trunk, and use a little less. Day one thousand forty-eight.

1049.title: Hospices and prisons
1049.hook: Buddhist chaplains and volunteers in hospices and prisons
1049.howItsDone: Buddhist chaplains serve in some hospitals, hospices and prisons, and lay volunteers and monastics visit the dying and lead meditation groups behind bars, some describing the work as being present rather than fixing.

segments.voice: Yesterday, saffron cloth around a trunk, and a forest marked for care. Your line: the ordained tree. Did you find your tree? Day one thousand forty-nine.

A heavy door buzzes. A guard checks a list, then waves through a woman carrying a small round cushion under her arm. Down the hall, in a plain room with plastic chairs, a handful of men in prison clothes are waiting for her. Across town, at the same hour, a volunteer pulls a chair close to a hospice bed and doesn't say anything at all for a while. Two very different rooms. In both, someone from this path has come to sit with people in hard places. Today we ask where that comes from.
screen: `A CUSHION THROUGH THE PRISON DOOR.` → `A CHAIR BY A HOSPICE BED.` → `SITTING IN HARD PLACES.`

segments.voice: Start with a story from the Vinaya. The Buddha and Ananda, walking through the monks' lodgings, find a monk sick with dysentery, lying in his own mess, and no one is caring for him. The other monks say he was no use to them, so they left him. The Buddha sends Ananda for water. The Buddha pours, Ananda washes, and together they lift the man onto a bed. Then the Buddha gathers the monks and says, in paraphrase: you have no mother and no father here to look after you. If you don't tend one another, who will? Whoever would tend me, let him tend the sick. Then a story that speaks to prisons. The Majjhima Nikaya tells of Angulimala, a man the text calls a murderer, who meets the Buddha, stops, and becomes a monk. People still fear him. When he goes begging, stones are thrown and he comes back bleeding, and the Buddha tells him to bear it: the results of what he did are ripening. The story doesn't erase the harm. It does refuse to say a person is beyond change. Those two stories help explain the modern work. Buddhist chaplains serve in hospitals and hospices, and some volunteers lead meditation groups in prisons. Some describe their task as presence more than fixing. At a deathbed, they may simply sit with someone's breathing, or with a frightened family. Behind bars, a sitting group may be one of the few quiet rooms in the building. None of it makes hard places easy. It brings a steady person into them.
screen: `A SICK MONK, LEFT ALONE.` · `WHOEVER WOULD TEND ME, TEND THE SICK.` · `ANGULIMALA, AND THE STONES.` · then, large: `PRESENCE MORE THAN FIXING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, if you'd like: hold one person in a hard place. Sit, and let the breath slow. Bring to mind someone in a hospital, a care home, a prison, or a long grief. If no one comes, hold all of them, wherever they are. Breathe in, and picture yourself sitting near them, not talking, just there. Breathe out, and wish them steadiness. Then, before the bell, choose one small, real help: a card, a call, a visit, a donation to a group that visits. Keep it small enough to do this week. The bell holds the time.
Gilana. The sick monk the Buddha washed with his own hands, whose care stands behind the chaplains and volunteers who now sit with people in hospices and prisons. Today's word.

Your line: in hard places. Today, when someone tells you something heavy, resist the urge to fix it right away. Pull up a chair, in whatever way you can, and stay a little longer. Day one thousand forty-nine.

1050.title: Temples of the diaspora
1050.hook: immigrant temples as homes far from home
1050.howItsDone: Some Buddhist communities who have moved abroad have built temples, from rented rooms to large buildings, where they keep festivals, teach children the chants and language, support resident monastics and welcome newcomers.

segments.voice: Yesterday, chaplains and volunteers sitting with the gilana, the sick, in hospices and prisons. Your line: in hard places. Did you pull up a chair for someone? Today closes a week. Day one thousand fifty.

This week walked through some hard and hopeful ground: the debate over women's ordination, trust broken and faced, mindfulness in offices, monks in labs, robes on trees, chairs pulled up to hospice beds. Now a quieter scene. A house on an ordinary street, in a city far from Asia. Shoes are piled by the front door. Inside, the living room has become a shrine room, and the kitchen smells of rice and curry. Children in the back room are learning letters their grandparents grew up with. Today, the temples people built when they moved far from home.
screen: `A WEEK OF HARD AND HOPEFUL GROUND.` → `SHOES PILED BY THE DOOR.` → `A HOUSE BECOMES A TEMPLE.`

segments.voice: When families from Sri Lanka, Thailand, Vietnam, Laos, Cambodia, Tibet, Korea, Japan and elsewhere settled in new countries, some of them built temples, often starting small. A rented room. A house. A building that used to be something else. Sometimes a monk was invited from home to live there. And the temple quickly became more than a place to sit. It's where a festival is kept on the right moon. Where a child learns the chants and the old language. Where a newborn is blessed, a wedding is honored, and a funeral is held in a way that feels right. Where a newcomer finds someone who knows how to fill out the forms. The Sigalovada Sutta lays out what a lay follower and the renunciants he supports, monks among them, owe each other, in paraphrase: lay people keep their doors open and offer what renunciants need; renunciants teach, steer people from harm, and show the way. In a diaspora temple, that old exchange is easy to see. The community feeds the monk, and the monk helps hold the community together. These temples also carry real strains. Children grow up speaking a different language than their elders. Some temples offer one service in the old language and a meditation class in English, and the two groups don't always meet. Some communities are working on that, and some aren't yet. An old line in the Dhammapada, in Max Müller's translation, fits these places: "trust is the best of relationships." A temple far from home runs on trust, and it builds it too.
screen: `A RENTED ROOM, A HOUSE, A MONK INVITED.` · `MORE THAN A PLACE TO SIT.` · `DOORS OPEN, THE WAY SHOWN.` · then, large: `TRUST IS THE BEST OF RELATIONSHIPS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, if you'd like: welcome someone new. Sit, and let the breath settle. Remember a time you were the new one: a new school, a new job, a new country, a new street. Who made it a little easier? What did they do? Let the memory stay a moment. Then bring to mind someone new near you now: a neighbor who just moved in, a new coworker, a family at your children's school. Picture one small welcome you could give them. A name learned. A tip about the town. A plate of food. The bell holds the time.
Vihara. A dwelling, and so a temple, built by people who moved far from home, where the chants, the festivals, the old language and the community are kept alive. Today's word.
Your line: a home far from home. Today, learn the name of one person who's new around you, and use it the next time you see them. Day one thousand fifty.
